Richard Baxter
RICH-erd BAKS-ter
proper noun
English Puritan pastor (1615–1691); Baxter, an occupational surname from the Old English bæcestre, a baker.

See also: Richard Baxter

📖 Biblical Definition

Richard Baxter was the Puritan pastor of Kidderminster whose labors transformed a careless town into a praying congregation, and whose The Reformed Pastor (1656) remains the church’s great manual of pastoral diligence—not “reformed” in the doctrinal sense but in the sense of a renewed, watchful ministry that catechizes every family and takes heed to the whole flock. His The Saints’ Everlasting Rest turned the believer’s eye to the heavenly rest that remains for the people of God, and his A Call to the Unconverted pressed sinners with tender urgency. Baxter ministered through plague and civil war, was ejected in the Great Ejection of 1662, and suffered imprisonment under a hostile bench for his nonconformity. Yet the dictionary cannot follow Baxter in all his doctrine. On justification he departed from the Reformed standard into a scheme—later called Baxterianism or neonomianism—that made faith and evangelical obedience a new law whose performance is counted for righteousness, softening the imputed righteousness of Christ that the Reformation recovered. His view of the atonement leaned toward the universal-payment scheme. The dictionary honors Baxter’s pastoral fire and his suffering for conscience while naming his justification error as a real departure from the gospel of grace alone.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

English Puritan pastor (1615–1691); author of The Reformed Pastor and The Saints’ Everlasting Rest; honored for pastoral diligence, corrected for his neonomian view of justification.

expand to see more

RICHARD BAXTER, Puritan pastor of Kidderminster (1615–1691).

Wrote The Reformed Pastor, the great manual of watchful, catechizing ministry.

Wrote The Saints’ Everlasting Rest, turning the soul to the heavenly rest.

Ejected in 1662 and imprisoned for nonconformity, suffering for conscience.

Held a neonomian view of justification the dictionary names as error.

📖 Key Scripture

Act 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Heb 4:9 — "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God."

Rom 3:28 — "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Baxter’s pastoral writings are rightly loved, but his neonomian doctrine of justification—making faith and obedience a new law counted for righteousness—corrupted the imputed righteousness of Christ.

expand to see more

The corruption is Baxterianism itself: the scheme that the gospel is a “new law” whose terms are faith and sincere obedience, and that God accepts the believer’s evangelical obedience as his righteousness rather than imputing to him the perfect righteousness of Christ. This softens justification by faith alone into a covenant of milder works, and it confuses the ground of acceptance (Christ’s obedience reckoned ours) with the fruit of it (our obedience flowing from faith). The Reformation recovered that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law; Baxter’s scheme reintroduces the deeds, however refined, into the ground of standing before God.

The principle to recover is the clean Reformed doctrine of justification: Christ’s active and passive obedience imputed to the believer, received by faith alone, apart from any works of our own. Baxter’s pastoral diligence is to be imitated; his justification error is to be refused. A faithful ministry presses men to holiness while resting their whole acceptance on the righteousness of Another.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Puritan pastor of Kidderminster (1615–1691); great on pastoral labor, erring on justification (neonomianism).

Richard Baxter — Puritan pastor and author (1615–1691).

The Reformed Pastor — the manual of catechizing, watchful ministry (Act 20:28).

The Saints’ Everlasting Rest — the heavenly rest of God’s people (Heb 4:9).

Ejected 1662; suffered imprisonment for nonconformity.
